newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro bourses, dollar lower on the day.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro bourses, dollar lower on the day.

text.p: U.S. data which eased inflation fears helped stem losses on European bourses on Tuesday, while prompting gains by U.S. bonds and on Wall Street, but leading European markets still ended well into the minus column.

The dollar showed a fairly muted reaction to the latest American data but had earlier lost some of its shine after Germany's top economic institutes forecast healthy German economic activity and a possible rise in interest rates there.

Lower-than-expected third quarter U.S. labour cost figures and a fall in the October consumer confidence index brought some encouragement that U.S. interest rates, which set wider trends, might not have to rise just yet to keep inflation in check.
But markets on both sides of the Atlantic were nervous ahead of yet more statistics giving clues on the state of the world's biggest economy later in the week.
"I think the important figures are to come. Tomorrow we have third-quarter U.S. GDP and obviously non-farm payrolls on Friday," said the head of trading at a leading investment bank in London.

Wall Street, the world's biggest stock market watched keenly by markets elsewhere, fluctuated within a 39-point range centred on the Dow Jones industrial average's previous close in the first two hours of trading.
By noon in New York it was just a few points ahead and dealers said it was constrained by uncertainty over this week's data and next week's U.S. Presidential election.

Just as the Dow had receded back below its key 6,000 level, London's FTSE 100 index slipped below its 4,000 landmark amid re-awakening fears of a rise in British interest rates following stronger-than-expected British money supply figures.
However, dealers said Wednesday's monthly monetary meeting between the British finance minister and the governor of the Bank of England was unlikely to produce a rate rise.
A sharp reverse on Wall Street on Monday and jitters over interest rates had undermined European stock markets from the start, prompting losses that exceeded one percent in some cases.
In Frankfurt, shares lost more than one percent due to uncertainty over interest rates, Wall Street's decline and a weaker dollar, which made less pleasant news for exporters.
French stocks fell 1.15 percent due to weakness in the dollar and bond prices and concern that German interest rates might rise, affecting those elsewhere.
The German institutes said the country's 1997 public deficit was likely to exceed its target for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Currency dealers said this provided a reminder of the struggle European countries could have in meeting tough economic criteria for EMU. This was seen as another bullish signal for the mark, Europe's key currency at present.
In contrast, a barrage of comments from German officials left the overall feeling that there was still a possibility of a further easing in German monetary policy, dealers said.

In Asian trading, the dollar had hit a new 42-month high of 114.88 yen against a Japanese currency weakened by a search by Japanese investors for higher-yielding investments abroad and political uncertainty after recent elections.
The U.S. currency later headed lower, as it weakened against the mark, before topping 114 yen again by the European close.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was around 1.5100 marks and 114.02 yen versus 1.5207 and 114.26 in late European business on Monday. It earlier fell as low as 1.5061 and 113.50.
STOCKS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares ended 31.8 points lower at 3,993.5.

Germany's 30-share DAX index finished bourse floor trade 30.21 lower at 2,673.62 but showed little net change in later electronic business, ending at 2,675.50. In Paris, the CAC-40 share index closed down 24.65 at 2,125.74.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold ended London trading at $381.50 an ounce, down from a fix of $381.70 in the afternoon, a morning fix of $382.35 and Monday's London close of $383.35. Silver fell eight cents to $4.85.
